identity.name: Konbaung dynasty
native_names: ကုန်းဘောင်ခေတ်

predecessors.note: The Mon kingdom of Lower Burma (1740-1757), which Cliopatria draws under the Konbaung name for 1741-1756. It also held Ava and Upper Burma from March 1752 to January 1754 after ending the Toungoo dynasty. No dossier exists; see notes.
The Toungoo (Nyaungyan, Ava) dynasty ended at Ava in March 1752 (first-toungoo-empire dossier); the Konbaung took Upper Burma from the Hanthawaddy conquerors, not from the Toungoo.

land.text: the Cliopatria row 'Burma' (1820-1884): the same Konbaung state under Bagyidaw

successors.note: The Konbaung dynasty reigned to 29 November 1885 (infobox); Cliopatria cuts its row at Bodawpaya's death in 1819 and continues the state as 'Burma'. The burma dossier of another batch should carry the Konbaung kings from 1819.

capitals.name: Amarapura

correction.text: empty: the Konbaung dynasty does not exist before 29 February 1752; this Lower Burma shape is the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom's (1740-1757)

keyframe_review.note: 1741-1751, 116,344 km2: Ayeyarwady, Bago, Yangon, Mon and Kayin, i.e. Lower Burma. The page: 'the Mon of Lower Burma broke away in 1740, and founded the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom' and 'by 1745, Hanthawaddy had successfully established itself in Lower Burma'. The Konbaung dynasty starts on 29 February 1752 (infobox of the Konbaung dynasty page); the shape is Hanthawaddy land and belongs to a dossier Cliopatria lacks (restored-hanthawaddy-kingdom, 1740-1757).

correction.text: Alaungpaya's Moksobo/Shwebo, capital 1752-1760, where he rose against the Hanthawaddy besiegers of Ava

keyframe_review.note: 1752-1756, 112,429 km2: still Lower Burma (Ayeyarwady, Bago, Mon, Kayin) plus 36 per cent of Mandalay, i.e. Hanthawaddy with the Ava region it held from March 1752. The Konbaung proper in 1752 is the Shwebo (Moksobo) core; 'By late 1753, Konbaung forces controlled all of Upper Burma except Ava' and Ava was retaken on 3 January 1754. The correction gives the 1752 core; new keyframes 1753, 1754 and 1755 follow.
New keyframe, 1753: 'By late 1753, Konbaung forces controlled all of Upper Burma except Ava.' The 'Upper Burma' region is my reading of the page's phrase.

The Sino-Burmese War page adds that 'In 1754, Burma reacquired the nearer Shan States'. The Hanthawaddy counter-invasion of March-May 1754 failed. [Repaired 2026-10-19 after review: the whole of Shan State is replaced by the nearer Shan states only (the Shan cells of the 1757 shape); 'Nearer Shan States had been reacquired since 1754' (Sino-Burmese War page) and the sawbwas gave homage 'as far north as Momeik' (Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War page).]

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1755-1756: 'Konbaung forces invaded Lower Burma in January 1755, capturing the Irrawaddy Delta and Dagon (Yangon) by May'; Syriam fell on 26 July 1756. Pegu, Martaban and the east of Lower Burma are still Hanthawaddy's until May 1757. [Repaired 2026-10-19 after review: whole Shan State replaced by the nearer Shan states, as in 1754.]

1757-1761, 446,707 km2: Upper Burma plus Lower Burma, with the Shan, Chin and Kachin margins. Starts in the year Pegu fell: 'On 6 May 1757' the final assault; infobox 'Konbaung annexes Lower Burma down to upper Tenasserim peninsula'. The page calls Konbaung control of upper Tenasserim in 1757-1759 'largely nominal'; the shape rightly leaves it out. Infobox area: only 794,000 km2 for 1824. [Author repair 2026-10-19: the farther Shan states and the Kachin hills are not in this shape (65 per cent of Shan, 41 per cent of Kachin); they join as a tributary from 1759 (ledger vassal_start), so the shape stands unchanged.]

keyframe_review.note: 1762-1768, 522,158 km2: adds Lan Na (Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai, Lampang, Lamphun, Phayao) and the Mon and Kayin remainder. Lan Na was conquered 'in 1762-1763' and 'Chiang Mai fell to the Burmese invaders' in August 1763, so the shape starts a year early for Lan Na; and 'Maha Nawrahta ... quickly took Mergui and Tenasserim on 11 January 1765' so Tenasserim joins in 1765, four years before the next Cliopatria shape. Correction for 1762: the shape without Lan Na; new keyframes 1763 and 1765 follow.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1767 only (added after review). 'Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese on 7 April 1767'; Nemyo Thihapate 'stayed in the ruins until his departure in June 1767'; Phraya Tak 'reconquered Ayutthaya-Thonburi area in November 1767'. Ayutthaya dissolved on 7 April 1767 (ayutthaya-kingdom ledger) and Thonburi was founded in December 1767, so the interval is recorded as a gain from Ayutthaya and a loss to Thonburi, not as an occupation of a state that no longer existed. 1768 returns to the 1765 outline.

1769-1774, 669,238 km2: the full shape with Shan, Kachin, Tenasserim and Lan Na. After the Treaty of Kaungton 'Burma remained in possession of Koshanpye' (nine states above Bhamo); Kengtung was Burmese. The Sino-Burmese page puts the border 'roughly at its pre-1730s position' and leaves it undemarcated. Infobox area: none for 1769. [Repaired 2026-10-19 after review: verdict ok -> adjust. The shape adds 35 per cent of Shan and 57 per cent of Kachin (about 100,000 km2) over the 1765 outline, with no gain in the ledger; the Sino-Burmese War page has Alaungpaya's expedition of 1758-59 'to the farther Shan States' to 'reestablish Burmese authority' and the Konbaung dynasty page has the Shan and Kachin principalities as tributary fiefdoms, 'never directly controlled', so those cells are taken out of the direct-land shape and carried by the 1759 vassal_start (the burma dossier tints the same lands from 1820). Lampang and Lamphun cells added as in 1763.]

region.text: Moksobo/Shwebo, the home of the village chief who became Alaungpaya

ledger.note: 29 February 1752: Alaungpaya founds the Konbaung dynasty at Shwebo. Infobox 'Start: 29 February 1752'; 'In 1752, a village chief (later Alaungpaya) founded the dynasty to challenge the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom.' Capital Shwebo 1752-1760.

region.text: the Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War begins

ledger.note: 20 April 1752: the Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War begins. The page dates the war '20 April 1752 - 6 May 1757'; Alaungpaya beats a Hanthawaddy detachment at Halin on 20 April 1752 and 'on 20 June 1752 ... routed the besiegers'; Ava had fallen to Pegu on 22 March 1752 (first-toungoo-empire dossier).

region.text: all of Upper Burma except Ava

ledger.note: 1753: Upper Burma but Ava is Konbaung. 'By late 1753, Konbaung forces controlled all of Upper Burma except Ava.'

region.text: the nearer Shan states: the Shan cells of Cliopatria's 1757 Konbaung shape (65 per cent of Shan State, as far north as Momeik)

ledger.note: 1754: the nearer Shan states return to Burma. 'Nearer Shan States had been reacquired since 1754' (Sino-Burmese War page, reopened); after Ava was retaken on 3 January 1754 Alaungpaya 'turned to nearer Shan States to secure the rear, and to draw fresh levies' and 'received homage from the nearer sawbwas (saophas or chiefs) as far north as Momeik' (Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War page). Region: the Shan cells of Cliopatria's 1757 shape (65 per cent of Shan State), my reading of 'nearer'; the farther states follow as the 1759 vassal_start. Counterpart nobody: the shan-states dossier ends in 1563 and the sawbwas are not a state. The Konbaung dynasty page says the Shan states 'paid tribute' and were 'never directly controlled', so treating the nearer states as direct land rests on 'reacquired' (confidence 2). [Repaired 2026-10-19 after review: was the whole of Shan State with counterpart shan-states.]

region.text: Upper Burma is secure

ledger.note: 1754: Upper Burma is secure. The Hanthawaddy offensive of March-May 1754 failed, and the plot of the captive Toungoo king was crushed in October 1754; the war moves south in January 1755.

region.text: Ava (Inwa)

ledger.note: 3 January 1754: Hsinbyushin retakes Ava. 'On 3 January 1754, Alaungpaya's second son, Hsinbyushin, only 17, successfully retook Ava.' The Hanthawaddy counter-invasion followed in March 1754 ('sent the entire army') and in May Alaungpaya led his armies himself.

region.text: the invasion of Lower Burma

ledger.note: January 1755: the invasion of Lower Burma. 'By January 1755, he was ready to launch a full-scale invasion of the south'; 'Konbaung forces invaded Lower Burma in January 1755, capturing the Irrawaddy Delta and Dagon (Yangon) by May.'

region.text: the Irrawaddy Delta and Dagon (Yangon)

ledger.note: 5 May 1755: the Irrawaddy Delta and Dagon fall. 'On 5 May 1755, Konbaung troops defeated a Hanthawaddy division at Dagon'; Rangoon was founded in 1755 as a fortress and harbour (Konbaung dynasty page).

region.text: Syriam (Thanlyin), the French-garrisoned port across the river from Dagon

ledger.note: 26 July 1756: Syriam falls and French involvement ends. 'At the dawn of 26 July 1756, after bloody hand-to-hand fighting they managed to pry open the great wooden gates'; 'fell in July 1756, ending French involvement in the war'.

region.text: Pegu falls

ledger.note: 6 May 1757: Pegu falls. 'On 6 May 1757' the Konbaung armies broke through at Pegu (Bago) and sacked the capital; infobox 'Konbaung annexes Lower Burma down to upper Tenasserim peninsula'. The governors of Martaban and Tavoy then sent tribute, but control of upper Tenasserim stayed 'largely nominal' in 1757-1759.

region.text: the Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War ends in a 'Decisive Konbaung victory'; the last king of Hanthawaddy was executed in 1774 and Mon revolts followed in 1758, 1762, 17

ledger.note: 6 May 1757: the Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War ends in a 'Decisive Konbaung victory'; the last king of Hanthawaddy was executed in 1774 and Mon revolts followed in 1758, 1762, 1774, 1783, 1792 and 1824-1826.

region.text: war with Siam over the Tenasserim coast

ledger.note: 1759: war with Siam over the Tenasserim coast. 'The Konbaung armies seized the upper Tenasserim coast following the Burmese-Siamese War (1759-1760)'; the Konbaung dynasty page: 'In 1760, Burma began a series of wars with Siam lasting into the mid-19th century.'

region.text: the farther Shan states and the Kachin hills (Koshanpye): the Shan and Kachin cells of Cliopatria's 1769 shape that are not in its 1757 shape

ledger.counterpart: Farther Shan states and northern Kachin
ledger.note: 1758-59: Alaungpaya brings the farther Shan states and the Kachin hills back under Burmese authority. 'In 1758-59, King Alaungpaya ... sent an expedition to the farther Shan States' (annexed by the Qing 'over two decades earlier') 'to reestablish Burmese authority' over 'present-day Kachin State and northern and eastern Shan State' (Sino-Burmese War page, reopened). The page gives the aim, not the result. The Konbaung dynasty page has the Shan, Palaung and Kachin principalities as tributary fiefdoms, 'never directly controlled', the burma dossier tints the same lands from 1820, and after Kaungton (13 December 1769) 'Burma remained in possession of Koshanpye, the nine states above Bhamo'; so the relation is drawn as tribute (vassal tint), contested with the Qing from December 1765 to December 1769 (events below). The Qing, who held the sawbwas' allegiance before, is not the counterpart: the vassal is. Region: the Shan and Kachin cells of the 1769 shape that are not in the 1757 shape, my reading of 'farther' (190 Shan and 186 Kachin cells). No vassal_end: the relation continues under the burma dossier (vassal_start 1820). [Added 2026-10-19 after review: the 1769 shape had these lands with no event.]

region.text: Tavoy and the upper Tenasserim coast

ledger.note: 1760: upper Tenasserim is Burmese. 'The Konbaung armies seized the upper Tenasserim coast following the Burmese-Siamese War (1759-1760)' (the ayutthaya-kingdom dossier has Dawei and upper Tenasserim lost in April 1760 and Alaungpaya dying in May 1760).

region.text: the first Burmese-Siamese war ends with Alaungpaya's death; Ayutthaya is not taken.

ledger.note: 1760: the first Burmese-Siamese war ends with Alaungpaya's death; Ayutthaya is not taken.
1760: the capital moves from Shwebo to Sagaing (infobox: Sagaing 1760-1765).

region.text: Lan Na, Chiang Mai and the northern Thai cities

ledger.note: 1762: the conquest of Lan Na begins. 'Burma sent forces to successfully conquer Lanna Chiang Mai in 1762-1763.'

region.text: Tavoy

ledger.note: Late 1763: Tavoy rises and returns to Siam. 'Udaungza rose up and seized power in Tavoy,' and Tavoy returned to Siamese rule after this.

region.text: Lan Na, Chiang Mai and the northern Thai cities

ledger.note: August 1763: Chiang Mai falls to the Burmese. Chiang Mai 'held until August 1763 when Chiang Mai fell to the Burmese invaders'; Nemyo Thihapate left to subdue the rest of Lanna in February 1764.

region.text: Lan Na, Chiang Mai and the northern Thai cities

ledger.note: 1763: Lan Na is Burmese; the lords of Lan Na serve as Burmese governors until the Siamese take Chiang Mai in January 1775.
1765: the capital moves from Sagaing to Ava (infobox: Ava 1765-1783).

region.text: Tenasserim

ledger.note: January 1765: Tenasserim. Maha Nawrahta 'sent his vanguard of 5,000 men to take Tavoy in January 1765' and 'quickly took Mergui and Tenasserim on 11 January 1765'; 'Siam lost Tenaserim to Burma for perpetuity in 1765.'

region.text: the kingdom of Luang Prabang

ledger.note: March 1765: Luang Prabang becomes a Burmese vassal. 'Luang Prabang fell to the Burmese in March 1765' and the Lao kingdoms 'then became Burmese vassals in 1765'; Vientiane's Ong Boun had urged the invasion in October 1764. Kingdom of Luang Phrabang page: 'Burmese vassal, 1765-1768' for Sotika-Kuomane.

region.text: the kingdom of Vientiane

ledger.note: March 1765: Vientiane becomes a Burmese vassal. Nemyo Thihapate 'conquered Lao kingdoms of Luang Prabang and Vientiane in March 1765'; Kingdom of Vientiane page: 'a Burmese vassal from 1765 to 1779'.

region.text: Northern and Central Siam, the Chao Phraya basin to Ayutthaya

ledger.note: 23 August 1765: the Burmese invasion of Siam. The Burmese-Lanna-Lao army 'left Lampang on 23 August 1765' for Northern Siam; the war runs '23 August 1765 - 7 April 1767' (infobox).

region.text: the Shan states and the Bhamo country on the Yunnan border

ledger.note: December 1765: the first Qing invasion. Liu Zao ordered an invasion of Kengtung 'in December 1765,' which the Burmese defeated; three more invasions followed in 1766-1769 (Bhamo, Hsenwi, Singu, Maymyo). The Burmese 'occupy eight Chinese Shan states within Yunnan' in 1767.

region.text: Ayutthaya and the Chao Phraya basin

ledger.note: 7 April 1767: Ayutthaya falls and the Burmese hold the ruins. 'Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese on 7 April 1767'; Nemyo Thihapate 'stayed in the ruins until his departure in June 1767'. Recorded as a gain from Ayutthaya, which dissolves on 7 April 1767 (ayutthaya-kingdom ledger, counterpart thonburi-kingdom): the Burmese garrison held the land, they did not annex it, and no state owned it in the interval. [Repaired 2026-10-19 after review: was an occupation_start naming ayutthaya-kingdom, a state that no longer existed to record the owner side.]

region.text: Northern and Central Siam

ledger.note: 7 April 1767: the Burmese-Siamese War of 1765-1767 ends with the fall of Ayutthaya; Hsinbyushin had ordered his besiegers in January 1767 'to finish up the conquest of Ayutthaya' so he could face the Qing.

region.text: Ayutthaya and Thonburi

ledger.note: November 1767: Taksin retakes the capital region. Phraya Tak 'reconquered Ayutthaya-Thonburi area in November 1767' and was enthroned as King Taksin in December 1767; the Burmese keep only Tenasserim (infobox: 'by 1770, only Tenasserim remains under Burmese control'). Recorded as a loss to Thonburi, whose found event of December 1767 takes the area (thonburi-kingdom ledger). [Repaired 2026-10-19 after review: was an occupation_end naming ayutthaya-kingdom.]

region.text: the Shan states and the Bhamo country on the Yunnan border

ledger.note: 13 December 1769: the Treaty of Kaungton ends the Sino-Burmese War. 'At Kaungton, on 13 December 1769 (or 22 December 1769)' the sides signed; 'Burma remained in possession of Koshanpye, the nine states above Bhamo', and kept authority over southern Yunnan borderlands as far as Kenghung (Chiang Huang, until 1886).

region.text: Chiang Mai and the Lan Na core of the Chiangmai row, without the Burmese-held Chiang Rai country

ledger.note: January 1775: the Siamese take Chiang Mai. 'The Siamese were able to take Chiang Mai in January 1775' (Taksin's expedition of late 1774); Lan Na passes to Thonburi's client Chiang Mai (chiangmai dossier). The Burmese counterattacked from Chiang Saen in September 1775 and failed. Chiang Rai (Chiang Saen) is not part of this loss: 'the Burmese regrouped and reestablished their headquarters at Chiang Saen' (Thonburi page) and it stays Burmese until 1804 (ledger). Lampang and Lamphun go to Thonburi itself (next event). [Repaired 2026-10-19 after review: region was all of Lanna.]

region.text: the Lampang and Lamphun cells of the Thonburi shape, Lan Na land that Cliopatria draws in no Konbaung shape

ledger.note: January 1775: Lampang and Lamphun pass to Thonburi. 'Thonburi took control of Lanna in 1775, ending the 200 years of Burmese vassalage' and Taksin appointed Kawila governor of Lampang in 1775 (Thonburi page, reopened); the thonburi-kingdom ledger records the matching gain. The page does not name Lamphun; the cells are the part of both provinces that Cliopatria gives to the Thonburi shape rather than to the Chiangmai row (confidence 2). [Added 2026-10-19 after review: the 1775 loss is split between chiangmai and thonburi-kingdom.]

region.text: Sawankhalok, Sukhothai and Phitsanulok

ledger.note: October 1775: the Burmese invade northern Siam. 'Maha Thiha Thura marched his massive army of 35,000 men from Martaban through the Mae Lamao Pass into Northern Siam in October 1775' and 'quickly took Sawankhalok and Sukhothai'; Phitsanulok fell in March 1776 and was destroyed.

region.text: Sawankhalok, Sukhothai and Phitsanulok

ledger.note: August 1776: the Burmese leave Siam. 'The Burmese had left Siam by August 1776'; Hsinbyushin had died on 10 June 1776 and Singu Min succeeded him. Result: 'Siamese victory; depopulation of Northern Cities and destruction of Phitsanulok'.

region.text: the kingdom of Luang Prabang

ledger.note: 1778: Luang Prabang passes under Siam. Kingdom of Luang Phrabang page: status 'Vassal of Siam (1778-1893)'; the same page's ruler list keeps 'Burmese vassal, 1768-1788' for Surinyavong II, which I treat as an error of the infobox.

region.text: the kingdom of Vientiane

ledger.note: 1779: Vientiane passes from Burma to Siam. 'The kingdom was a Burmese vassal from 1765 to 1779'; 'In 1779, Siamese forces sacked Vientiane ... Ong Boun decided to submit to the Siamese and Vientiane became a Siamese dependency.'
1783: Bodawpaya moves the capital to Amarapura (infobox: Amarapura 1783-1821).

region.text: the invasion of Arakan begins

ledger.note: 2 December 1784: the invasion of Arakan begins. 'The invasion then commenced on December 2, 1784'; the Burmese camped at Laungkyet on 31 December 1784.

region.text: Mrauk U falls and Arakan is annexed

ledger.note: 2 January 1785: Mrauk U falls and Arakan is annexed. '...they captured the Arakanese capital, Mrauk-U, on January 2, 1785'; infobox 'Arakan is annexed under the Konbaung dynasty of Burma'. The Konbaung dynasty page has 'Bodawpaya acquired Arakan in 1784' in its text and 1785 in its infobox; about 35,000 Rakhine fled to Chittagong afterwards (undated).

region.text: the Arakan campaign ends with the capture of Mrauk U; the Burmese invasions of Siam in 1785 and 1786 'failed' (Konbaung dynasty page) and moved no border.

ledger.note: January 1785: the Arakan campaign ends with the capture of Mrauk U; the Burmese invasions of Siam in 1785 and 1786 'failed' (Konbaung dynasty page) and moved no border.

union.text: Tavoy
Mergui

region.text: Tavoy and Mergui, the lower Tenasserim coast

ledger.note: 1792: Tavoy and Mergui pass to Siam. 'The defection of Burmese governor of Tavoy to Siam in March 1792' gave Siam its opportunity, Yommaraj Bunnag took Tavoy over and Mergui followed (Burmese-Siamese War 1792-1794 page, reopened); the page gives no month for the takeover. The rattanakosin-kingdom ledger has no matching gain for 1792 and dates the Burmese recovery to 1793 (see notes). [Added 2026-10-19 after review.]

union.text: Tavoy
Mergui

region.text: Tavoy and Mergui, the lower Tenasserim coast

ledger.note: 16 January 1794: the Burmese retake Tavoy. 'The Siamese were soundly defeated in the Battle of Tavoy in January 1794 and retreated' (assault of 16 January 1794, when the townspeople opened the gates); Mergui's governor 'decided to defect back to the Burmese side'. The page describes no cession; the infobox has Tenasserim 'within the Burmese sphere of influence'. The Rattanakosin page's 'ceded for perpetuity' in 1793 (rattanakosin-kingdom ledger) is a year earlier than this page's battle. [Added 2026-10-19 after review.]

region.text: Chiang Saen and the Chiang Rai country, Burmese-held until 1804

ledger.note: 1804: Chiang Saen falls to Chiang Mai. 'Chiang Mai forces under Thammalangka managed to capture Chiang Saen in 1804' (Chiang Mai page, reopened), where the Burmese had their headquarters from 1775; the Burmese-Siamese wars table dates the war 1802-1805 with Chiang Saen the territorial change. Matches the 1804 gain in the chiangmai ledger. [Added 2026-10-19 after review.]

region.text: the kingdom of Manipur

ledger.note: 1814: Bodawpaya annexes Manipur. 'He acquired Manipur in 1814 and Assam in 1817, creating a long border with British India'; Manipur is 'later annexed by Bodawpaya in 1814'. The admin-1 unit stands for the kingdom of Manipur.

region.text: Ahom Assam, occupied from 1817

ledger.note: 1817: Assam. 'He acquired Manipur in 1814 and Assam in 1817'; Burma ceded Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim to Britain in 1826 (First Anglo-Burmese War).

region.text: the Konbaung state in 1819, continued as Cliopatria's Burma 1820

ledger.note: 1819: Cliopatria's 'Konbaung Dynasty' row ends with Bodawpaya (infobox 'Bodawpaya, 1782-1819') and the state continues as the 'Burma' row; the dynasty itself reigned until 29 November 1885. Page silent on any break in 1819-1820.

wars.name: Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War
wars.outcome: Decisive Konbaung victory: Ava retaken on 3 January 1754, Dagon and the delta in May 1755, Syriam on 26 July 1756, Pegu on 6 May 1757; Lower Burma annexed down to upper Tenasserim.
wars.note: 20 April 1752 - 6 May 1757 (infobox). French arms and ships backed Hanthawaddy.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1759-1760)
wars.outcome: The Konbaung armies seized the upper Tenasserim coast; Ayutthaya was not taken. Alaungpaya died in 1760.
wars.note: Only the Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War page was opened for this war: 'seized the upper Tenasserim coast following the Burmese-Siamese War (1759-1760)'.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1765-1767)

zones.text: Lan Na, Chiang Mai and the northern Thai cities

wars.outcome: Burmese victory: Tenasserim lost to Burma in 1765, Lan Na held from August 1763, Luang Prabang and Vientiane vassals from March 1765, Ayutthaya fell on 7 April 1767; Taksin retook the Chao Phraya region in November 1767.
wars.note: Infobox: 23 August 1765 - 7 April 1767. 'By 1770, only Tenasserim remains under Burmese control.'

wars.name: Sino-Burmese War (1765-1769)

zones.text: the Shan states and the Bhamo country

wars.outcome: Burmese victory in four Qing invasions; Treaty of Kaungton, 13 December 1769. Burma kept the Shan states, Koshanpye and its sway over southern Yunnan as far as Kenghung; trade was reopened by the Qing in 1788 and relations resumed in 1790.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1775-1776)
wars.outcome: Siamese victory: Chiang Mai taken by the Siamese in January 1775; the Burmese invaded Northern Siam in October 1775, took Sukhothai and Phitsanulok and left by August 1776.

wars.name: Konbaung conquest of Arakan
wars.outcome: Burmese victory: Mrauk U captured on 2 January 1785 and Arakan annexed.

wars.name: Burmese invasions of Siam (1785-1786)
wars.outcome: The Burmese invasions of the reconstituted Siam in 1785 and 1786 failed (Konbaung dynasty page); no border moved.
wars.note: The Konbaung dynasty page gives no details for 1785-1786; the Burmese-Siamese wars table lists it as the Nine Armies' War, 'Burma tries to capture Siam, and is soundly defeated' (Siamese defensive victory, no territorial change). The chiangmai ledger has the Burmese siege of Lampang from Chiang Saen in 1785-1788. The table has no war of 1787 (checked 2026-10-19). [Repaired 2026-10-19: later wars added below.]

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1788)
wars.outcome: Burmese defensive victory: Siam tried to capture Tavoy and reclaim the Tenasserim coast and failed; no ground changed hands.
wars.note: Table entry 'Siamese Invasion of Tenasserim: Siam tries to capture Tavoy, and reclaim the Tenasserim coast but fails'. The page has no war of 1787.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1792-1794)

union.text: Tavoy
Mergui

zones.text: Tavoy and Mergui, the lower Tenasserim coast

wars.outcome: Burmese defensive victory: Tavoy's governor defected to Siam in March 1792 and Siam held Tavoy and Mergui; the Siamese were defeated at Tavoy in January 1794 and Mergui returned to Burma. The lower Tenasserim coast stayed Burmese.
wars.note: Infobox March 1792 - March 1794. The page describes no cession; the Rattanakosin page dates a cession 'for perpetuity' to 1793.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1797-1798)

zones.text: the Chiang Mai basin, besieged by the Burmese

wars.outcome: Siamese defensive victory: Burma invaded Lan Na and besieged Chiang Mai; Kawila asked Rama I for reinforcements; no ground changed hands.
wars.note: Table: 'Burma invades Lan Na and besieges Chiang Mai. The city was taken, but Kawila asks for reinforcement from Rama I'. The Chiang Mai page has Bodawpaya send 55,000 men to 'attack Chiang Mai in 1797'.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1802-1805)

zones.text: Chiang Saen and the Chiang Rai country, Burmese-held until 1804

wars.outcome: Siamese victory: Chiang Saen, the Burmese base in Lan Na, was taken by Chiang Mai forces in 1804.
wars.note: Table: 'Burma attacks Lan Na, but is defeated again', territorial change Chiang Saen (Lan Na). The Chiang Mai page dates the capture 1804.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1809-1812)
wars.outcome: Siamese defensive victory: Burma's attempts to capture Junk Ceylon (Thalang) were repelled in 1810 and 1812; no ground changed hands.
wars.note: Table: 'Burma unsuccessfully attempts to capture Junk Ceylon and is repelled in 1810 and 1812'.

certainty.note: No treaty line: the Kaungton settlement of 1769 left the Yunnan border undemarcated, the Shan and Lan Na frontiers are tributary margins, and the Tenasserim line to Siam is a pass line. The 1814 and 1817 gains in India are approximate.

notes:
Page budget 5; eight pages are cited because two (Luang Prabang, Vientiane) were opened for the Lao dossiers of this batch and give the end dates of the vassalages; six were opened for Burma itself (WebFetch summaries, so every quotation is the summariser's quotation).

Cliopatria's row. (1) Its first two shapes (1741-1751, 1752-1756; Ayeyarwady, Bago, Yangon, Mon, Kayin and, from 1752, 36 per cent of Mandalay) are the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom of Lower Burma (1740-1757), not Konbaung land; both are marked wrong and the real 1752-1756 Konbaung is given by four new keyframes (Shwebo 1752, Upper Burma without Ava 1753, with Ava and the nearer Shan states 1754, with the Irrawaddy Delta 1755-1756). The Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom has no Cliopatria row and no dossier: it is a counterpart that needs one (slug restored-hanthawaddy-kingdom, 1740-1757, Lower Burma, Pegu; the first-toungoo-empire dossier already uses that slug). (2) Lan Na enters the shape in 1762 but Chiang Mai fell in August 1763, and Tenasserim enters in 1769 but was taken in January 1765. (3) Rakhine enters in 1788 but Mrauk U fell on 2 January 1785. (4) The 1815 shape lacks Manipur (1814) and Assam (1817). (5) The row ends in 1819 although the dynasty reigned to 1885: the burma dossier (Cliopatria 'Burma' 1820-1989, Q836) should be read as the same state; I recommend treating konbaung-dynasty and burma as one state (colour and family) and I have ended this dossier at the row boundary.

Infobox area 794,000 km2 is for 1824; this row's maximum is 675,755 km2 (ratio 0.85), and Burma 1822 is 797,916 km2, so the comparison is fine once Manipur and Assam are added.

Pages disagree: Arakan 1784 (Konbaung dynasty text) or 1785 (infobox and the conquest page); Luang Prabang 'Burmese vassal 1765-1768' against '1768-1788' on the same page; Sino-Burmese War end 13 or 22 December 1769.

Not written: the ruler strip (the infobox lists only Alaungpaya 1752-1760, Hsinbyushin 1763-1776 and Bodawpaya 1782-1819, missing Naungdawgyi and Singu Min, whom the opened pages mention only in passing). Manipur is said to have been 'reunited' with Burma by 1759 and the Shan states to have paid tribute 'at various times' without dates, so no vassal events are written for them. Counterparts without dossiers: manipur (kingdom of Manipur), ahom-kingdom (Assam), restored-hanthawaddy-kingdom, kingdom-of-kengtung and the Koshanpye states.

Repair after review (2026-10-19). Pages reopened: Sino-Burmese War, Konbaung dynasty, Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War, Burmese-Siamese War (1775-1776), Thonburi Kingdom, Kingdom of Chiang Mai, the table of Burmese-Siamese wars, Burmese-Siamese War (1792-1794), Kingdom of Manipur. (1) The 1754 gain now names the nearer Shan states only (the Shan cells of the 1757 shape) with counterpart nobody. (2) New vassal_start of 1759 for the farther Shan states and northern Kachin (tributary, counterpart a string for the tributary states), and the 1769 to 1815 keyframes lose those cells; the burma dossier tints the same lands from 1820. I partly disagree with the review on the nearer states: the Konbaung dynasty page says all the Shan states were 'never directly controlled', so a uniform tint for Shan State would be more faithful and would match burma's 1820 vassal_start; I kept the nearer states as direct land because the Sino-Burmese War page says 'reacquired' and the Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War page records homage, and the orchestrator can move that event to a vassal_start and subtract the nearer cells from the keyframes. The Sino-Burmese War page does not say whether the 1758-59 expedition succeeded, so the 1759 event is confidence 2 and the Koshanpye 'possession' of 1769 is the only evidence of the result. (3) Chiang Saen: Chiang Rai is added to the 1775, 1785, 1788 and 1794 keyframes (to 1803), a new 1804 keyframe drops it, and the 1804 loss to chiangmai mirrors the chiangmai gain; the 1775 loss is split between chiangmai (the Chiangmai row without Chiang Rai) and thonburi-kingdom (the Lampang and Lamphun cells, which are now also in the 1763-1774 keyframes because Cliopatria's Konbaung shapes did not hold them). (4) Tavoy and Mergui: loss to rattanakosin-kingdom in 1792 and gain in January 1794, with a 1792-1793 keyframe; the 1792-1794 page dates the Burmese recovery to January 1794 and describes no cession, whereas rattanakosin-kingdom /ledger/9 has the cession in 1793 and has no 1792 gain (for the Rattanakosin author, se-01-j). Wars added: 1788, 1792-1794, 1797-1798, 1802-1805, 1809-1812 (table of Burmese-Siamese wars); the table has no 1787 war; the Kingdom of Manipur page dates no Burmese campaign between 1758 and 1770 (it says only that Manipur was 'occupied by the Kingdom of Burma' after 1751), so no Manipur war is written. (5) The 1767 occupation is now a gain from ayutthaya-kingdom (April 1767) and a loss to thonburi-kingdom (November 1767) with a one-year keyframe; the thonburi-kingdom found event of December 1767 is the mirror. (6) The 1819 dissolve at confidence 1 is a Cliopatria row boundary (the dynasty reigned to 1885), unchanged here: konbaung-dynasty and burma should share one colour and family, or the orchestrator should merge the rows. Not done (thin, for a gap-filler): the ruler strip (the Konbaung dynasty page now gives Alaungpaya 1752-1760, Naungdawgyi 1760-1763, Hsinbyushin 1763-1776, Bodawpaya 1782-1819; Singu and Phaungka are undated there) and the Manipur and Assam vassal reading.
